items.title: 63476_Jimmie Crawford oral history interview
items.q: I asked Cozie, I said, how do you execute that? So he told me.

ctx.x: I guess I was a natural. I finally heard -- I'm jumping a little bit. I finally heard Cozy Cole playing a solo known as Ratamacue. That's what it sounded like, Ratamacue. And Paradiddles is the name of it, paradiddle, paradiddle. In other words, paradiddle, paradiddle, see how my hands are going? Right, left, right, right, left, left, so on. So I asked Cozie, I said, how do you execute that? So he told me. It's in there in the book. I said, what book?
And I got this book that I learned how to do my ratamakes and the paradiddles. Rolls, I always had some kind of rolls. And I did that. And so --

items.title: 53342_Cozy Cole oral history interview
items.q: See, and all I wanted Specs Powell to just play the tympany, Jimmy Crawford just to play that cymbal.

ctx.x: Just to cover one or two more odds and ends, there's in, I'm looking right now at an article that Dan Morgenstern did on you for Downbeat in the March 20, 1969 issue, it was a very nice article, and he mentioned that you had done another record with four drummers for Choral with Bobby Rosengarden, Specs Powell and Jimmy Crawford. That's before the one that you did with Krupa and Ray McKinley.

And Panama, that's right. We had all different rhythms on this other one that I did. Well one of them was that "Big Noise from Winnetka." See, and all I wanted Specs Powell to just play the tympany, Jimmy Crawford just to play that cymbal. Bobby Rosengarden to play the 6-8 time, and me I'd just weave in between all of them.
So was it all pretty successful?
